title: THE SIN YOU HIDE IN SHAME… AND THE SINS THE CHURCH APPLAUDS IN PUBLIC
paragraphs: THE SIN YOU HIDE IN SHAME… AND THE SINS THE CHURCH APPLAUDS IN PUBLIC

Why Do Some Christians Treat Masturbation as Worse Than Pride, Cruelty, or Dishonesty? What If Jesus Is More Concerned About the Heart We Refuse to Examine Than the Struggle We Are Terrified to Confess?
There is a young man sitting alone on the edge of his bed tonight.
His Bible is open. His phone is beside him. His eyes are burning.
He has fallen into a sexual habit he promised God he would never repeat.
Again.
He whispers, “Lord, I'm sorry.”
But this time, something feels different.
He cannot bring himself to look at the Bible.
He wonders whether God is disgusted with him.
Whether his prayers still matter.
Whether he has finally exhausted the mercy of Jesus Christ.
And somewhere across town, another Christian is sleeping peacefully.

That man spent the afternoon humiliating his wife. He lied to protect his reputation. He mocked someone weaker than himself. He refused to apologize because, in his mind, admitting fault would make him look small.
He will attend church tomorrow.
He will raise his hands during worship.
He might even criticize the young man if he ever discovers his private struggle.
And perhaps the most disturbing part of this story is not that both men have sinned.
It is that one is terrified of his sin while the other has learned to feel righteous inside his.
How did we reach a place where some Christians tremble over private sexual struggles but barely flinch at pride, cruelty, dishonesty, or the destruction they leave in other people's hearts?
Before you answer, understand something.
This is not an article defending masturbation as automatically righteous, harmless, or spiritually insignificant.
It is not an invitation to excuse lust, pornography, compulsive behavior, or sexual choices that violate a person's conscience.
And it is certainly not an attempt to make sexual holiness irrelevant.
This is something more uncomfortable.
It is an invitation to examine whether we have confused the sins that embarrass us with the sins that most offend God.
Because Jesus did not come merely to make respectable sinners feel superior to ashamed sinners.
He came to save sinners.
Including the ones who have learned to disguise their rebellion as righteousness.
And that truth may confront us more deeply than we expect.
There is a passage in Scripture that should make every religious person uncomfortable.
In Luke 18:9–14, Jesus tells a parable about two men who enter the temple to pray.
One is a Pharisee.
The other is a tax collector.
The Pharisee stands confidently and thanks God that he is not like other people. He lists his religious accomplishments, including fasting and tithing.
The tax collector stands at a distance.
He will not even lift his eyes toward heaven.
He beats his chest and cries:
“God be merciful to me a sinner.” — Luke 18:13, KJV
The original Greek makes this scene even more striking.
The man's prayer contains the words:
ὁ θεός, ἱλάσθητί μοι τῷ ἁμαρτωλῷ
Ho Theos, hilasthēti moi tō hamartōlō.
A faithful rendering is:
“God, be merciful to me, the sinner.”
The Greek verb hilasthēti carries the sense of seeking God's merciful favor in relation to sin. It is more than a casual request to overlook a mistake.
This man knows he cannot make himself righteous.
He needs mercy.
And then Jesus delivers the conclusion that overturns the expectations of everyone listening.
The tax collector goes home justified rather than the Pharisee.
Why?
Because the Pharisee was satisfied with himself.
The tax collector was crying out for God.
Jesus was not teaching that dishonest tax collecting was acceptable.
He was exposing the danger of self-righteousness.
And this is where our conversation about sexual shame must begin.
The person who knows he needs forgiveness may be closer to repentance than the person who believes he has nothing serious to confess.
Think about that.
A believer may struggle with sexual temptation and sincerely desire holiness.
Another may abstain from every sexual behavior his community condemns while regularly belittling his children, manipulating his spouse, spreading rumors, and treating struggling people with contempt.
Which person is spiritually healthy?
We cannot determine that from one behavior alone.
And neither should we pretend that sexual restraint cancels cruelty.
The Bible never gives us permission to exchange one kind of holiness for another.
It calls us to become holy in the whole of our lives.
Yet sometimes Christian communities become exceptionally skilled at policing sexuality while remaining strangely tolerant of sins that destroy relationships.
A harsh father is described as strict.
A controlling leader is called strong.
A dishonest businessman is praised for being successful.
A proud church member is admired for having high standards.
A gossip is dismissed as someone who is merely concerned.
But a believer who admits a private sexual struggle may immediately be treated as spiritually contaminated.
Why?
Part of the answer is that sexual behavior is surrounded by powerful emotions: modesty, shame, vulnerability, family expectations, and religious teaching.
Another part is that visible rules are easier to enforce than inward transformation.
It is easier to condemn a behavior than to confront the pride that makes us enjoy condemning people.
It is easier to demand purity from someone else than to admit how often our own words have been cruel.
And sometimes the sins we condemn most loudly are the sins that threaten our public image least.
Jesus knew this tendency.

In Matthew 23:23, He rebuked religious leaders for carefully attending to certain religious obligations while neglecting what He called the weightier matters of the law: justice, mercy, and faithfulness.
He did not tell them to abandon obedience.
He told them not to neglect the greater demands of God's character while concentrating on outward religious precision.
Then, in Matthew 23:25–28, He exposed the tragedy of appearing clean externally while remaining corrupt internally.
Imagine hearing that from Jesus Himself.
You have spent years making sure people see you as religious.
And the Son of God tells you that the inside of your life is the very place requiring repentance.
That is not a comfortable message.
But it is a saving one.
Because the Jesus who exposes hypocrisy is also the Jesus who calls hypocrites to repentance.
Now we must confront the question many Christians are afraid to discuss plainly.
Does the Bible explicitly say masturbation is a sin?
The answer requires care.
There is no biblical passage that directly names masturbation and universally declares the physical act itself sinful.
That does not mean every instance is morally neutral.
It means we must distinguish what Scripture explicitly teaches from conclusions Christians draw through broader biblical principles.
For example, Matthew 5:27–28 records Jesus teaching that looking at another person with lustful intent is a matter of the heart, not merely outward conduct.
The Greek word ἐπιθυμῆσαι (epithymēsai) refers here to desiring or coveting in the context of Jesus' warning against adultery.
Jesus is addressing a deliberately cultivated desire directed toward someone in a way that violates the moral meaning of the commandment.
He is not saying that every involuntary sexual feeling is equivalent to committing adultery.
That distinction matters.
Sexual attraction is not automatically the same as lustful intent.
Temptation is not automatically the same as consent.
And the presence of bodily desire does not, by itself, prove that someone has abandoned God.
James 1:14–15 describes how desire can entice a person and, when embraced and developed into sin, bring forth destructive consequences.
The passage calls us to take temptation seriously.
But it also helps us avoid treating the experience of temptation as identical to deliberate sinful action.
The apostle Paul teaches that the body matters to God.
In 1 Corinthians 6:18–20, he calls believers to flee sexual immorality and honor God with their bodies.

The Greek term πορνεία (porneia) refers broadly to sexual immorality. Its precise applications must be established through biblical context and moral reasoning; the word itself is not a direct reference to masturbation.

Christians therefore disagree about whether masturbation is inherently sinful, sinful under particular circumstances, or morally permissible when separated from lust, pornography, coercion, and other harmful factors.
Some Christian traditions regard it as contrary to God's design for sexuality.
Others distinguish the physical act from the intentions, fantasies, habits, and consequences surrounding it.
These disagreements should not be hidden.
Nor should they become excuses for dismissing conscience.

Romans 14:23 reminds believers that acting against one's conviction before God is spiritually serious. Although Paul is addressing disputed practices in a different context, the principle encourages careful discernment rather than careless self-justification.
A Christian who believes a particular behavior is sinful should not be pressured to violate that conviction.
But a Christian teacher should also be cautious about declaring, “God explicitly said this,” when the biblical text does not explicitly say it.
Faithfulness to Scripture requires us to be as careful about what God has not directly stated as we are about what He has clearly commanded.
That is not compromise.
That is reverence.
And perhaps this is where someone reading needs to hear something important.
You are not helped by being told that every sexual impulse makes you filthy.
You are not helped by being told that your body is inherently disgusting.
You are not helped by confusing shame with sanctification.
But neither are you helped by pretending your choices have no spiritual meaning.
The Gospel offers a better way than either panic or permissiveness.
It calls you into truth.
If pornography has become part of your life, do not minimize its power to shape your desires, distort your view of other people, or become a compulsive escape from loneliness.
If sexual behavior has become your way of numbing anxiety, grief, rejection, or emotional pain, pay attention to what you are trying not to feel.
If you are repeatedly violating your conscience, do not silence it simply because someone tells you that nothing matters.
And if your struggle has become compulsive or is seriously affecting your daily life, seeking qualified professional help alongside trusted spiritual support is not a failure of faith.
But please hear this as well.
You do not need to manufacture self-hatred to prove that you love Jesus.
Repentance is not the same as despising your existence.
Conviction identifies what needs to change.
Toxic shame tells you that you are beyond redemption.
The Holy Spirit leads people toward truth and transformation.
Despair tells them there is no point in returning.
Those are not the same voices.
And this distinction becomes even more important when we remember what Scripture says about the sins we sometimes excuse.
Proverbs 6:16–19 describes things the Lord hates.
The passage begins with:
“A proud look, a lying tongue, and hands that shed innocent blood.” — Proverbs 6:17, KJV
The Hebrew expression behind “a proud look” is עֵינַיִם רָמוֹת (ʿênayim rāmôt), literally referring to elevated or haughty eyes.
It describes arrogance expressed through the way a person regards others.
The list also includes a heart devising wicked plans, a false witness speaking lies, and a person who sows discord among others.
Notice what is happening.
God is not merely concerned with what someone does privately.
He is concerned with the person who lies.
The person who plots harm.
The person who spreads division.
The person who looks down on others.
The person whose behavior damages the lives around them.
And pride is especially dangerous because it can hide inside religion itself.
A person can be proud of avoiding pornography.
Proud of never masturbating.
Proud of following every outward rule.
Proud of being more disciplined than everyone else.
And slowly, without recognizing what has happened, that person may begin to love the feeling of being morally superior more than the God who calls us to humility.
This does not make sexual holiness unimportant.
It means holiness without love becomes a contradiction of the very character Christians are called to reflect.
Paul makes the warning unmistakable in 1 Corinthians 13:1–3.
Even extraordinary spiritual gifts, religious sacrifice, and impressive acts of devotion amount to nothing without love.
And in Galatians 5:19–23, he places sexual immorality among the works of the flesh while also identifying hostility, jealousy, fits of anger, rivalries, divisions, and envy.
The same passage describes the fruit of the Spirit as love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control.
Read that again.
Self-control matters.
So does kindness.
Faithfulness matters.
So does gentleness.
Sexual conduct matters.
So does the way you speak to someone who has disappointed you.
The Spirit does not produce holiness in one isolated corner of a person's life while giving permission for cruelty everywhere else.
And perhaps the question we should ask is not merely, “Have I avoided this sexual behavior?”
Perhaps we should also ask:
“Am I becoming more truthful?”
“Am I becoming more compassionate?”
“Do people feel safer or more wounded after encountering me?”
“Have I apologized to the people I have hurt?”
“Do I treat the struggling with the same mercy I hope God will show me?”
“Am I using religious rules to avoid confronting the ugliness of my own pride?”
Those questions are uncomfortable.
But they are deeply biblical.
And they bring us to one of the most revealing encounters in the ministry of Jesus.
In John 8:1–11, religious accusers bring before Jesus a woman accused of adultery.
The scene is filled with public shame.
The woman stands exposed.
Her accusers stand ready to condemn.
And Jesus challenges those without sin to cast the first stone.
One by one, they leave.
Then Jesus tells the woman:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.” — John 8:11, KJV

There is an important textual detail here. The account of the woman caught in adultery, John 7:53–8:11, is absent from some of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts of John's Gospel. Many modern Bible translations identify this manuscript question. Christians have long treasured the account, but responsible interpretation should acknowledge its textual history rather than conceal it.
The scene nevertheless expresses a distinction found throughout the undisputed teachings of Jesus.
Mercy is not permission to continue in sin.
And the call to repentance is not permission to humiliate a sinner.
Jesus does not celebrate adultery.
He does not join the crowd in destroying the woman.
He refuses to make public condemnation the final word over her life.
That distinction should change the way Christians speak about sexual struggles.
A church can teach chastity without cruelty.
A pastor can preach repentance without humiliation.
A parent can guide a child toward sexual integrity without teaching that the child's body is disgusting.
A believer can confess a struggle without being treated as a spectacle.
And a Christian community can take sexual ethics seriously while also confronting abuse, greed, dishonesty, racism, exploitation, gossip, pride, and spiritual manipulation.
We do not have to choose between holiness and mercy.
In Jesus Christ, we are called to both.
But there is another person I want to speak to now.
Not the young man sitting on his bed.
Not the person overwhelmed by sexual guilt.
I want to speak to the Christian who has never considered himself part of this problem.
The one who reads articles like this and immediately thinks of somebody else.
Perhaps you have never struggled with masturbation.
Perhaps sexual discipline has come more easily to you than it has to others.
That may be something for which you can sincerely thank God.
But have you ever enjoyed hearing that someone else failed?
Have you ever used another person's confession to feel better about yourself?
Have you ever spoken about someone's private struggle in a way you would never want your own failures discussed?
Have you ever withheld kindness because you believed a person was spiritually beneath you?
Have you ever been more concerned about a church's reputation than about the wounded person standing in front of you?
Because if you have, this conversation is not merely about somebody else's sexual behavior.
It is about your heart, too.
And mine.
And the hearts of all of us who need the mercy of Jesus Christ.
Romans 3:23 declares:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.” — KJV
All.
Not merely those who struggle sexually.
Not merely those who are publicly exposed.
Not merely those whose sins are considered embarrassing.
All.
The preacher.
The worship leader.
The parent.
The church volunteer.
The person who has never missed Sunday worship.
The person who has not attended church in years because shame convinced them they were no longer welcome.
We do not all struggle in the same ways.
We are not all responsible for identical actions.
And different sins can have different consequences for victims, relationships, and communities.
But none of us can stand before God on the strength of our own flawless record.
That is why the Gospel is such astonishing news.
Jesus did not come because humanity needed a little improvement in public behavior.
He came because sinners needed reconciliation with God.
He lived in perfect obedience.
He died for our sins.
He rose again.
And through Him, forgiveness and new life are offered to those who turn to God in faith.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” — KJV
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we had repaired every weakness.
Not after we had earned the right to approach Him.
Not after we had become impressive enough to deserve His attention.
Christ died for sinners.
And that includes the person who has been hiding behind a respectable religious image.
It also includes the person who is frightened to pray because of what happened last night.
Listen carefully.
The cross does not tell us that sin is insignificant.
It tells us that sin is so serious that our redemption required the self-giving sacrifice of Jesus Christ.
But it also tells us that God's grace is greater than the hopelessness that sin can produce.
And if we truly believe that, we must stop treating certain struggling people as though they are uniquely beyond the reach of mercy.
First John 1:9 offers this promise:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — KJV
Notice that Scripture does not say some unrighteousness.
It says all.
Pride needs cleansing.
Dishonesty needs cleansing.
Cruelty needs cleansing.
Sexual immorality needs cleansing.
Self-righteousness needs cleansing.
And the God who calls us to confess is faithful.
Not because our repentance purchases forgiveness.
But because forgiveness rests upon the saving work of Jesus Christ.
This is where real transformation begins.
Not when a person becomes sufficiently terrified of being exposed.
Not when someone learns to perform religious perfection.
Not when a church develops an impressive list of forbidden behaviors.
Transformation begins with the grace of God bringing us into truthful surrender.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that God's grace trains believers to reject ungodliness and live self-controlled, upright, godly lives.
Grace does not simply comfort us while leaving everything unchanged.
Grace teaches us to live differently.
It helps the proud become humble.
The dishonest become truthful.
The cruel become gentle.
The sexually undisciplined grow in self-control.
The ashamed discover that they can come into the light without pretending they were never wounded.
And the religiously self-satisfied learn to say something they may have forgotten how to say.
“Lord, have mercy on me.”
Perhaps that is the prayer some of us need tonight.
Not a speech explaining why our sins are smaller than somebody else's.
Not another promise made out of panic.
Not a desperate attempt to negotiate with God.
Just a truthful confession.
“Jesus, You know what I have hidden.
You know what I have justified.
You know the desires I struggle to understand.
You know the people I have hurt.
You know the pride I have disguised as conviction.
You know how tired I am of pretending.
Please forgive me.
Teach me to love what is good.
Teach me to turn away from what destroys.
And teach me to see other people through the mercy You have shown me.”
If that prayer sounds painfully familiar, you are not alone.
And perhaps this is the moment to stop measuring your spiritual life only by the sins you have managed to avoid.
Ask instead whether you are walking toward Jesus.
Are you learning to tell the truth?
Are you becoming more willing to repent?
Are you making restitution where you have harmed someone?
Are you learning to respect your own body and the dignity of others?
Are you becoming more patient, gentle, faithful, and loving?
Are you allowing Scripture to correct you even when the correction threatens your favorite assumptions?
Because the Christian life is not a competition to see who can appear the cleanest.
It is a life of repentance, faith, obedience, and growing conformity to Jesus Christ.
And no one graduates from needing His grace.
Maybe you have spent years believing that your sexual struggle is the single greatest thing separating you from God.
Maybe it is a serious area of your life that requires repentance, accountability, or healing.
Take that seriously.
But do not ignore everything else God may be calling you to surrender.
Maybe the unforgiveness you have nurtured for years needs to be confronted.
Maybe your dishonesty needs to end.
Maybe the way you speak to your spouse needs to change.
Maybe your children need an apology more than another lecture.
Maybe you have been using religious language to justify controlling behavior.
Maybe you have confused being feared with being respected.
Maybe you have condemned others for visible struggles because you were unwilling to examine your own hidden motives.
And maybe, just maybe, the most important question you can ask tonight is not, “Am I worse than other Christians?”
It is this:
“Jesus, what in me still refuses to look like You?”
That question can change a life.
Because when Christ becomes our standard, superiority loses its appeal.
We stop asking whether our sins are more socially acceptable than someone else's.
We begin asking whether our lives are being transformed by His grace.
We stop using shame as a weapon.
We begin speaking truth in love.
We stop confusing spiritual maturity with the ability to condemn.
We begin recognizing it in humility, integrity, self-control, courage, compassion, and faithful obedience.
And if you are the person who opened this article because you feel ashamed of your private sexual struggle, I want you to remember one final thing.
Your struggle deserves honest examination.
Your conscience deserves careful attention.
Your choices matter.
But you are not beyond the reach of Jesus Christ.
Do not allow secrecy to become your prison.
Do not allow repeated failure to convince you that repentance is pointless.
And do not allow someone else's hypocrisy to become your excuse for abandoning holiness.
Bring the whole truth to Jesus.
Not only the behavior you are ashamed of.
Bring Him the loneliness.
The fear.
The resentment.
The pride.
The secret grief.
The anger.
The longing to be loved.
The places where you have wounded others.
And the places where you have been wounded yourself.
You do not need a carefully edited version of your life to approach the Savior.
He already knows the truth.
And He calls you to come into the light.
That is the heart of Gospel Warrior.
Not making sinners famous for their failures.
Not making religious people comfortable in their pride.
But continually pointing broken, struggling, imperfect human beings back to the crucified and risen Jesus Christ.
Not because scandal is good.
Not because sin has no consequences.
Not because repentance can be replaced by comforting words.
But because Jesus Christ is able to redeem lives that human beings would rather discard.
And this message is too important to remain trapped on one person's screen.
Somewhere on your Facebook friends list is someone who has quietly concluded that God is finished with them.
Somewhere is a Christian who has confused public respectability with spiritual maturity.
Somewhere is a parent who needs to learn how to correct without humiliating.
Somewhere is a struggling believer who has never heard anyone distinguish temptation from deliberate sin.
And somewhere is a person who has been so deeply wounded by religious condemnation that even hearing the name of Jesus now feels painful.
Not to embarrass anyone.
Not to start another argument.
But to open a conversation that many people are too afraid to begin.
Before you leave, I want to invite you into something more personal.
Have you ever felt that Christians were quicker to condemn sexual struggles than pride, dishonesty, or cruelty?
Have you ever been made to feel that your worst struggle was your entire identity?
Or have you realized that you were more willing to confront another person's weakness than your own?
You do not need to reveal private details or expose someone else's story.
And if you have experienced His restoring mercy, consider sharing a testimony of how Jesus has taught you to walk in truth and grace.
Your words may help another person find the courage to seek God rather than retreat further into shame.
And if this ministry has strengthened your faith, I also want to invite you to help carry the work forward.
Gospel Warrior is building and sharing resources to help people study Scripture, confront sin honestly, understand grace, and grow in biblical discipleship.
Those resources are meant to help people pursue a faith that continues beyond a single emotional moment on social media.
A faith that reads.
A faith that learns.
A faith that repents.
A faith that endures.
A faith that follows Jesus when no one is watching.
You do not have to pay to receive His grace.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not arise from reluctance or compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not guilt.
Not pressure.
Gratitude, generosity, and shared mission.
These items can serve as reminders of faith, encouragement, and opportunities to begin meaningful conversations about Christ.
It is helping sustain a ministry committed to sharing Scripture, calling people to repentance, proclaiming forgiveness in Jesus Christ, and encouraging believers to grow in their faith.
Read.
Pray.
Invite someone.
Encourage a struggling believer.
Send this article to a friend who needs hope.
The Gospel is not for sale.
Jesus Christ is not a product.
And grace cannot be purchased.
The question is not whether you have managed to hide your sins better than somebody else.
The question is whether you are willing to bring your whole life before Jesus Christ and allow His truth and grace to change you.
Because the man ashamed on the edge of his bed needs Jesus.
The religious man sleeping peacefully after hurting his family needs Jesus.
The person reading this while remembering a hidden failure needs Jesus.
And the person writing these words needs Jesus too.
We are not saved by having more respectable sins.
We are saved by grace through faith in Christ.
And the grace that saves us also teaches us to walk in newness of life.
So tonight, before you close this article, remember the tax collector who could barely lift his eyes toward heaven.
He had no impressive defense.
No record of superiority to present.
No polished explanation.
Only a desperate prayer for mercy.
And Jesus said that man went home justified.
What if the beginning of your healing is not finding a way to prove you are better than someone else?
What if it begins with finally telling Jesus the truth?
The most dangerous prison may not be the sin you are ashamed to confess, but the pride that convinces you there is nothing left to confess.
